title: Switching Costs
hook: Patient files grow roots when every allergy note, dosage change, and owner habit must move by hand.
counterintuition: The rival is not competing against price alone but against every field, routine, trust habit, and trained shortcut the customer would have to rebuild after leaving.
tryThisNow: Before accepting a cheaper alternative, list three things you would have to rebuild, retrain, or re-earn. Price the switch after those losses are visible.
keyTakeaway: Switching costs protect an incumbent when leaving would destroy or rebuild accumulated financial, procedural, or relational value the customer already relies on.

breakdown.fastRead:
"Show me where the allergy note goes," Fiona says, opening a patient file while the cheaper records contract waits beside a cancellation form. The new system costs less each month. It cannot carry dosage notes, owner preferences, or the warning that Luna reacts badly to one anesthetic.

Switching costs live in that gap. A rival offer has to beat the incumbent plus the pain of migration. If the customer loses setup, history, trust, training, or relationships by leaving, the incumbent has more than repeat business. It has continuity value.
breakdown.deepRead:
Fiona counts the fields the cheap system cannot carry before she signs the cancellation form. The monthly price difference is real. So is the work of rebuilding records, retraining staff, and risking one missed note in an exam room. The question is not whether the clinic likes the old software. The question is what leaving destroys.

Addiction is useful only as a signal. The customer stays because leaving breaks something already built, not because the old product is loved.

Switching costs can be financial, procedural, or relational. A printer may lose hours recalibrating color. A distributor may rebuild barcode rules in every frozen aisle. A school may have to persuade parents that new placement scores mean what the old ones meant. Each case asks the same question: what value must be rebuilt before the rival price is real?

Nicolas sees cyan drift under the light booth before he touches the calculator. The ink quote is lower, but the new workflow would require weeks of proofing old client jobs.

A lower invoice can still be an expensive exit.

Nicolas writes the discount in one column and the rebuilding work in the next. The second column is where weak switching-cost claims either earn their keep or collapse. If the client can carry the color settings, history, and proofing rules across in an afternoon, the lower quote wins more easily. If each job has to be re-earned by hand, the old vendor is protected by work the invoice does not show.
breakdown.fullRead:
The freezer fan rattles above aisle F while Kasia scans the first shelf after a warehouse software test. The scanner flashes red on a barcode rule the new vendor does not understand. The migration checklist says item locations will import cleanly. The frozen aisle says otherwise.

Switching costs are strongest when the customer has built value inside the incumbent system. That value may be data, routines, trained staff, supplier terms, trust, custom settings, or shared language with a service team. The more useful the accumulated setup becomes, the more a rival has to overcome before its lower price matters.

What exactly would you lose on the first day after leaving?

Hadiya learns the relational version from a parent email. Her language school can buy a cheaper placement test, but last year's placement notes carry meaning for teachers and families. Parents understand the old levels. Teachers know which score predicts a difficult first month. The new rubric may be better later, yet the school must rebuild confidence before the saving becomes clean.

The trap is calling every repeat purchase lock-in. A customer may buy again because the product is convenient, because nobody searched, or because habit carried the day. That is not switching cost by itself. The barrier appears when leaving imposes a concrete loss: money spent again, procedures rebuilt, relationships re-earned, risk absorbed during the move.

Portability weakens the barrier. If Astrid exports a building model and every door schedule, material tag, and revision note arrives cleanly in the rival design tool, the old library has less hold on the architecture firm. Standards, easy exports, and low setup burdens turn the rival price into a fairer comparison. The old provider may still be liked, but the lock loosens.

James sees the same issue in a municipal fleet garage. The cheaper parts supplier looks obvious until the shelf of unmatched filters appears on day three and warranty claims fall into a binder nobody trusts. The bid is not false. It is incomplete. The old supplier has continuity value because mechanics, part numbers, and warranty routines already fit together.

The practical move is to price the migration, not just the product. Count the records, the training, the broken handoffs, the trust conversations, and the risk period. Then compare. Sometimes the rival still wins. When it does, switching costs were never strong enough to protect the incumbent. When the migration burden overwhelms the headline savings, the incumbent's power is sitting in all the quiet work the customer would rather not do again.

This is why the best switching-cost test is practical rather than emotional. Do a small export. Rebuild one workflow. Ask one trusted user what would have to be rechecked before the switch feels safe. The pain you can point to is the barrier; vague reluctance is only a mood.

examples.title: Fiona counts the missing notes

planSpec.domain: veterinary clinic considering a cheaper patient-records system
planSpec.audience: clinic manager comparing software subscription savings against migration damage
planSpec.stakes: saving money may erase appointment history, dosage notes, and owner preferences
planSpec.requiredBeat: Fiona opens a patient file and counts the fields the cheap system cannot carry before she signs the cancellation form.

examples.scenario: "Show me where the allergy note goes," Fiona says, opening Luna's patient file while the cancellation form waits under her wrist. The cheaper records system promises a lower monthly fee, but the import preview drops dosage notes and owner preferences. Her pen stops above the signature line before the 3:00 p.m. staff meeting. She must decide whether the saving is real after the missing fields are rebuilt.
examples.whatToDo: Count every field, workflow, and risk that must move before signing. Compare the cheaper fee with the labor and clinical danger of rebuilding the patient history.
examples.whyItMatters: The rival price competes against the old system plus migration pain. If leaving destroys useful history, the incumbent has continuity value the invoice does not show.

examples.title: Nicolas sees cyan drift

planSpec.domain: commercial print shop moving from one color-calibration workflow to another
planSpec.audience: owner tempted by lower ink prices
planSpec.stakes: new vendor saves on supplies but forces months of recalibrating client jobs
planSpec.requiredBeat: Nicolas lays two proof sheets under the light booth and writes the lost calibration hours next to the lower ink quote.

examples.scenario: In the print shop light booth at 7:20 p.m., cyan looks wrong before Nicolas touches the calculator. Two proof sheets for the same museum catalog sit beside a lower ink quote from the new vendor. The quote saves money on every cartridge, but the gray balance from three repeat clients would need recalibration. Nicolas writes the lost hours next to the discount and must decide if the supplier switch is cheaper after color trust is rebuilt.
examples.whatToDo: Price the recalibration hours and client-proofing risk beside the ink savings. Change vendors only if the lower supply cost survives the procedural rebuild.
examples.whyItMatters: Switching costs hide in routines that already work. A cheaper input can be costly when it forces the customer to recreate calibration knowledge clients depend on.

examples.title: Kasia scans aisle F

planSpec.domain: regional food distributor changing warehouse management vendors
planSpec.stakes: the rival system is cheaper until every picker, barcode, and freezer location must be rebuilt
planSpec.requiredBeat: Kasia scans the first frozen aisle and marks every barcode rule that would have to be rebuilt before the new vendor goes live.

examples.scenario: The freezer fan rattles above aisle F while Kasia's barcode scanner flashes red for the third time. The freezer aisle map says the location imported. The migration checklist says the rule imported too. In the postmortem, she marks every picker shortcut, substitute code, and frozen-bin exception the new vendor missed before go-live and calculates the work the cheaper contract left out.
examples.whatToDo: Rebuild the migration estimate from the failed scan outward. Count barcode rules, picker routines, aisle exceptions, and training time before comparing vendors again.
examples.whyItMatters: Procedural value accumulates quietly. When a new system cannot carry those rules, the customer pays through errors and retraining instead of through the subscription line.

examples.title: Hadiya underlines the parent email

planSpec.domain: private language school replacing a long-time placement-test provider
planSpec.audience: school director weighing relational and procedural switching costs
planSpec.stakes: families trust the old test results and teachers have built lesson paths around them
planSpec.requiredBeat: Hadiya compares last year placement notes with the new test rubric and underlines the trust she would need to rebuild.

examples.scenario: It took Hadiya one parent call to see the real cost was not the invoice. Before the switch, teachers could read last year's placement notes and predict who needed extra speaking practice. After the trial, a parent email asks what the new B2 score means. Hadiya lays the old notes beside the new rubric and underlines every trust conversation the cheaper provider would force her to repeat.
examples.whatToDo: Treat parent confidence and teacher interpretation as migration work. Switch tests only after the school has a plan to translate old meaning into the new rubric.
examples.whyItMatters: Relational switching costs come from trust already earned. A cheaper test can be costly if families and teachers must relearn what the scores mean.

examples.title: James reveals the unmatched filters

planSpec.domain: municipal fleet garage switching maintenance parts suppliers
planSpec.audience: procurement lead comparing lower prices against continuity risk
planSpec.stakes: the lower bid matters only after cross-references, warranties, and mechanic routines survive the change
planSpec.requiredBeat: James has you pick the cheaper supplier, then reveals the shelf of unmatched part numbers that appears on day three.

examples.scenario: You notice the savings first and the unlabeled filters second. James places the supplier bid beside the warranty binder and asks you to pick the lower-cost parts vendor for the fleet garage. After you choose it, he opens a photo from day three: a shelf of unmatched part numbers and two mechanics waiting on cross-references. He must decide if the bid still wins after the routines break.
examples.whatToDo: Run the supplier bid through part-number matching, warranty handling, and mechanic workflow before awarding it. Count the day-three confusion as part of the switch price.
examples.whyItMatters: The incumbent supplier may be protected by continuity, not affection. Part numbers and warranty routines are value the garage would have to rebuild.

examples.title: Astrid circles the missing schedule

planSpec.domain: architecture firm leaving a proprietary model library
planSpec.audience: partner deciding whether portability weakens lock-in
planSpec.stakes: if templates export cleanly, the rival offer can be judged more directly; if not, the old system owns years of detail
planSpec.requiredBeat: Astrid exports one building model and circles every missing door schedule before comparing license prices.

examples.scenario: What exactly comes with you when you leave? At 4:45 p.m. in the architecture studio, Astrid exports a building model from the proprietary library and opens it in the rival tool. Walls arrive. Door schedules do not. Material tags scatter into blank fields. The license renewal is due Friday, and Astrid has to choose whether a lower subscription still wins after every missing schedule is rebuilt.
examples.whatToDo: Export a real model before judging license prices. If schedules, tags, and revision notes travel cleanly, the old provider has less lock-in; if not, price the rebuild.
examples.whyItMatters: Portability weakens switching costs. The easier it is to carry accumulated work into a rival system, the less protection the incumbent has.

questions.prompt: A clinic can save $600 a month by changing record systems. The import test loses allergy notes and custom dosage fields. What should the manager compare?
choices: Monthly fee against the cost and risk of rebuilding the missing clinical history
The old vendor's logo against the new vendor's logo
The number of staff who say they like the old system
questions.explanation: The saving is incomplete until migration loss is priced. Missing allergy and dosage data are continuity value. Logos and staff preference may matter, but they do not measure switching cost.

questions.prompt: A company buys from the same supplier every quarter because nobody has searched for alternatives. There are no custom settings, contracts, training, or relationship-specific routines. What does that show?
choices: Strong switching costs because repeat buying always proves lock-in
Weak evidence of switching costs because habit alone may explain the repeat purchase
Branding power because the supplier must be loved
questions.explanation: Repeat purchase is not enough. Switching costs require value that would be lost or rebuilt by leaving. Habit can create inertia without a durable barrier.

questions.prompt: A print shop wants cheaper ink, but changing vendors would force every museum catalog client through fresh proofing. Which cost category is most visible?
choices: Procedural switching cost from recalibrating work that already fits the old vendor
Network economy from adding more museum clients
Counter-positioning from a new business model
questions.explanation: The print shop must rebuild a workflow and client proofing routine. That is procedural migration pain. The prompt does not show user-to-user value or an incumbent self-harm trap.

questions.prompt: A design firm tests a rival tool and finds every model, tag, and schedule exports cleanly in an afternoon. What happens to the old provider's switching-cost barrier?
choices: It strengthens because the firm has used the old tool for years
It becomes branding automatically
It weakens because portability lowers the value lost during migration
questions.explanation: Clean portability reduces migration pain, so the rival price can be compared more directly. Long usage matters only if accumulated work is hard to carry forward.

questions.prompt: A school considers a cheaper placement test. Teachers understand the old levels and parents trust them. The new test is accurate but unfamiliar. What should the director price?
choices: Only the invoice difference between the two providers
The conversations and translation work needed to rebuild meaning around the new scores
The chance to advertise a modern test
questions.explanation: The school has relational and procedural value in the old scores. Accuracy may be real, but parents and teachers must relearn meaning before the saving is clean.

questions.prompt: A garage accepts a cheaper parts supplier and then discovers warranty claims, filter numbers, and mechanic routines no longer line up. What did procurement miss?
choices: Brand affection for the old supplier
The migration cost embedded in part-number matching and warranty routines
The need for a larger fleet
questions.explanation: The old supplier carried procedural continuity. The cheaper bid ignored the work of matching parts and warranties. Brand affection and fleet size are not the issue described.

questions.prompt: A project team wants to leave a collaboration tool. Files export easily, but five years of decision threads and client approvals are searchable only in the old account. Which response fits switching-cost logic?
choices: Leave immediately because file export proves all value moved
Stay forever because any old data creates permanent lock-in
Estimate the cost of preserving or rebuilding the decision history before comparing prices
questions.explanation: Some assets travel and others may not. The team should price the value trapped in searchable history. Easy file export lowers part of the barrier but does not erase every cost.

questions.prompt: A rival bank offers a higher savings rate, but a small business would need to rebuild payroll links, lender references, and merchant deposits. What keeps the incumbent bank protected?
choices: Financial and procedural switching costs tied to accumulated setup
Scale economies from having many branches
A network effect among all account holders
questions.explanation: Payroll, references, and deposits are accumulated setup that must be rebuilt. The prompt does not show declining unit cost from branch count or value moving among account holders.

questions.prompt: A software vendor claims customers are locked in because they renew every year. Customer interviews show exports are clean, onboarding takes one hour, and no custom history is stored. What should an analyst conclude?
choices: The vendor has strong switching costs because renewals prove it
The vendor has process power instead of switching costs
The switching-cost claim is weak unless another migration burden appears
questions.explanation: Clean exports and low setup burden weaken lock-in. Renewals may reflect satisfaction or inertia. Process power would require an embedded activity system, which the prompt does not show.

reviewCards.front: A rival offers a lower price. What must you retrieve before switching?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the value you would lose or rebuild: data, training, routines, relationships, setup, risk, and trust. The rival price is real only after migration pain is counted.

reviewCards.front: Why does repeat buying alone fail to prove switching costs?
reviewCards.back: A customer may repeat out of habit, convenience, or lack of search. Switching costs require a concrete loss or rebuild if the customer leaves.

reviewCards.front: What are the three broad kinds of switching cost to look for?
reviewCards.back: Financial costs, procedural costs, and relational costs. A customer may pay money, rebuild workflows, or re-earn trust and shared understanding.

reviewCards.front: How can portability weaken an incumbent's lock-in?
reviewCards.back: If data, settings, files, and workflows travel cleanly, the customer loses less by leaving. The rival offer can then compete more directly on price and product quality.

reviewCards.front: A school trusts an old placement test. What switching cost might a cheaper test ignore?
reviewCards.back: The trust and shared interpretation built around the old scores. Parents and teachers may need translation, reassurance, and time before the new test has the same value.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Use switching costs as a migration ledger. Before comparing products, write what the customer has already built inside the old system and what leaving would destroy or require them to rebuild.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a cheaper tool looks attractive, then I will run one real export and list every field, permission, and workflow that fails to carry over.
If a supplier bid is lower, then I will price cross-references, warranty handling, training, and exception work before awarding the contract.
If a school changes a trusted assessment, then I will plan how teachers and families will translate old meaning into the new score system.
If I switch banks, phones, or subscriptions, then I will list links, records, contacts, and habits that must be rebuilt before counting savings.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one service you keep using. List the three pieces of value you would lose or rebuild if you left, then decide whether the provider has real switching costs or mere habit.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, test one switching-cost claim by doing a mock migration: export, translate, or rebuild a small part of the setup and record what breaks.

memorableLines.text: A lower invoice can still be an expensive exit.
memorableLines.why: It makes the central comparison vivid and short.

memorableLines.text: What exactly would you lose on the first day after leaving?
memorableLines.why: It gives readers a practical diagnostic question.

memorableLines.text: The practical move is to price the migration, not just the product.
memorableLines.why: It states the chapter's operating rule in direct language.
